name: CoolTone
lead: CoolTone is a magnetic muscle-stimulation device from AbbVie, offered in clinics for toning and firming the abdomen, buttocks and thighs. A changing magnetic field makes the targeted muscles contract, and people use it, often alongside diet, exercise or fat-reduction treatments such as cryolipolysis (CoolSculpting), to get a firmer, more defined-looking midsection and lower body.[1][2][3]

According to the manufacturer, a session takes about 30 minutes, and the study it cites used 8 treatments over 4 weeks. The device is described as FDA-cleared for adults aged 22 and older to strengthen, tone and firm abdominal, buttock and thigh muscles, and for muscle spasm relief and leg stimulation in rehabilitation.[3]

Independent published evidence is limited. A small registered trial that began in 2022 with 15 participants compares CoolSculpting combined with CoolTone against CoolSculpting alone for the "banana roll" area beneath the buttocks; its status is listed as unknown and no results were found.[1] The manufacturer describes a 16-person study without a control group in which subjects who also followed diet and exercise plans roughly doubled plank hold time and raised crunch counts by 60% after a month.[3]

chain: Magnetic field triggers contractions in the abdomen, buttocks or thighs
Muscles are trained without conscious effort
angle.text: CoolTone is used to tone and firm muscles of the abdomen, buttocks and thighs without exercise effort, and some clinics pair it with fat freezing for a leaner, more defined shape.

infobox: Adults 22 and older, to strengthen, tone and firm muscles[3]

paras: CoolTone uses magnetic fields to induce muscle contractions, which the manufacturer says can enhance muscle function and act like muscle training.[3] A trial registration describes its use alongside CoolSculpting for the banana roll region, the fold of tissue under the buttock.[1] Cryolipolysis, the companion technology, uses controlled cooling to reduce localized subcutaneous fat; it was introduced in the United States in 2010 and its maker was acquired by Allergan in 2017.[2]

Electrical muscle stimulation, a related approach using skin electrodes, is established in rehabilitation and sports training, and Wikipedia reports it does not offer evidence of changing body shape or fat; the article does not cover magnetic devices.[4]

One registered trial (NCT05359614) compares CoolSculpting with CoolTone against CoolSculpting alone for the banana roll area in 15 participants. The trial began in March 2022, and its status is listed as unknown with no published results.[1] The manufacturer cites a small uncontrolled study of 16 subjects (14 completed follow-up) whose primary goal was patient perception of body shape.[3]

For the companion technology, a 2015 systematic review of 19 cryolipolysis studies reported skinfold reductions of 10.3% to 28.5%, and a 2023 review of 18 studies reported ultrasound-measured fat thickness reductions of 2.0 to 5.1 mm, with the authors describing the data quality as low.[2]

The manufacturer lists muscle pain, temporary muscle spasms, temporary joint or tendon pain and redness at the treatment site as common effects, and states it is not for people with metal or electronic implants such as pacemakers or defibrillators; pregnancy, hernia and IUD use call for caution or avoidance.[3] For cryolipolysis, reported effects include redness, numbness, swelling, bruising and mild pain, and paradoxical adipose hyperplasia, in which treated fat enlarges, has been reported in roughly 0.12% to 1.0% of cases depending on the study.[2]

timeline.event: A 15-person trial of CoolSculpting with CoolTone versus CoolSculpting alone begins.[1]

card.summary: A magnetic muscle-stimulation add-on to fat freezing, with almost no published evidence of its own.
card.note: Only one small registered trial found, with no results.

quick.overview:
CoolTone is a device that uses magnetic fields to make muscles contract, marketed for toning areas such as the lower buttock. It is discussed alongside fat-freezing treatments.

The only human study found is a 15-person registered trial, with no results available.
quick.mechanism: Magnetic muscle stimulation induces muscle contractions in the treated area; the intent is increased tone. No mechanistic study specific to CoolTone was found.
quick.risks: No CoolTone-specific safety data were found. The related fat-freezing procedure has reported side effects including redness, numbness, bruising and, rarely, paradoxical adipose hyperplasia.
